pll1d40c1-d1e3501.summary: States that predestination concerns saving goods and humans to be saved.

pll1d40c1-d1e3504.summary: Cites Augustine, De praedestinatione sanctorum: predestination is the preparation of grace, which cannot be without foreknowledge, but foreknowledge can be without predestination; by predestination God foreknew what he would do, but he also foreknew what he would not do, all evils.
claims: Predestination is the preparation of grace.

pll1d40c1-d1e3524.summary: States that God predestined those he chose and reprobated the rest, foreknowing they would sin unto eternal death.
claims: God reprobated those he foreknew would sin.

pll1d40c1-d1e3530.summary: States that none of the predestined can be damned and none of the reprobate saved.
claims: The predestined cannot be damned; the reprobate cannot be saved.

pll1d40c1-d1e3533.summary: Cites Augustine, De correptione et gratia, on Rev 3:11: if another will receive the crown only if this one loses it, the number of the elect is certain, that is, it cannot increase or decrease.
claims: The number of the elect is fixed.

pll1d40c1-d1e3565.summary: Reports the objection: God could withhold grace from those to whom he gives it, or give it to those he does not, so the number of the elect could decrease or increase.

pll1d40c1-d1e3570.summary: Answers that the number cannot change in the sense that both cannot be true together, that someone be saved and not predestined or predestined and damned. Taken simply, the impossibility does not hold. 'The predestined cannot be damned' is true conjointly, false disjointly, since he could have not been predestined.
claims: The fixity of the elect holds conjointly.
Taken disjointly, a predestined person could have been damned.

pll1d40c1-d1e3573.summary: Reports the further argument: it cannot be that one is predestined and damned; and it cannot now be that he is not predestined, since he was predestined from eternity; so he cannot be damned, and cannot not be saved.

pll1d40c1-d1e3576.summary: Says he would rather hear others than teach, but answers, as for foreknowledge, by distinguishing 'he cannot now not be predestined': conjointly true, but God could from eternity not have predestined him. Some grant that God can now not have predestined him, and so he can now not be predestined, though they deny this for deeds, since what has been done cannot not have been. For foreknowledge and predestination, possibility refers to God's power, which is always the same, since predestination, foreknowledge, and power are one in God.
claims: God could from eternity not have predestined someone.
For deeds, what is done cannot not have been.
For predestination, possibility refers to God's unchanging power.

pl-l1d40c1.summary: Treats predestination, which concerns saving goods and humans to be saved. With Augustine, predestination is the preparation of grace, which cannot be without foreknowledge, while foreknowledge can be without predestination, since God foreknows evils he will not do. God predestined those he chose and reprobated the rest, foreknowing they would sin. None of the predestined can be damned nor any reprobate saved, since the number of the elect is fixed (Rev 3:11). Against arguments that God could withdraw or add grace and so change the number, Lombard distinguishes: 'the predestined cannot be damned' is true conjointly (one cannot be both predestined and damned), false disjointly (this man could have not been predestined). Pressed further, he would rather hear others but answers that 'he cannot now not be predestined' is likewise ambiguous: God could from eternity not have predestined him. For foreknowledge and predestination, possibility refers to God's power, which is always the same.
claims: Predestination is the preparation of grace and presupposes foreknowledge.
Foreknowledge can exist without predestination, as with evils.
God predestined the elect and reprobated others, foreknowing their sins.
The number of the elect is fixed.
'The predestined cannot be damned' is true conjointly and false disjointly.
God could from eternity not have predestined someone.
For predestination, possibility is referred to God's unchanging power.
